title: Meeting Rooms II
statement: You get a list of meetings, each with a start time and an end time. Every meeting needs a room to itself while it runs. Return the smallest number of rooms that is enough. A meeting may start at the exact moment another ends and reuse its room.

example.caption: Three meetings are running at time 2 ([0,4], [1,3], [2,5]), so 3 rooms are needed.

idea.sentence: The answer is the most meetings running at once. Sort the starts and the ends separately and sweep: each start either finds a finished meeting to reuse or opens a room.

jargon.plain: An imaginary vertical line moved left to right across time. You react at each start and each end.
Two indexes moving forward through two sorted lists. Here one walks the starts, the other walks the ends.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a list of [start, end] pairs, e.g. [[0,4],[1,3],[2,5],[4,6],[5,6]]

compare.bruteLabel: For each start, count the meetings running
compare.optimalLabel: Sort starts and ends, then sweep

rows.name: Count at every start
rows.note: For each meeting start, count how many meetings contain that moment. Take the largest.

rows.name: Sorted starts and ends
rows.note: Two sorts dominate. The sweep is one pass with two indexes.

rows.name: Min-heap of end times
rows.note: Not shown. Sort by start, and keep the end times of busy rooms in a heap. Its size is the answer.

fast.takeaway: You never need to know which meeting uses which room. Only the count of overlaps matters, and two sorted lists give it.

stages.title: Sort both lists
stages.note: Collect all starts and all ends, and sort each list on its own with a numeric comparator.

stages.title: Next start vs earliest end
stages.note: Is this start strictly before the earliest end not yet reused? That decides whether anyone has left.

stages.title: Open a room
stages.note: Nobody has left yet, so this meeting needs a new room. The room count goes up.

stages.title: Reuse a room
stages.note: A meeting has ended, so its room is free. Move the end pointer on. The room count stays.

stages.title: Return
stages.note: The room count is the peak number of overlapping meetings.

edges.title: Back to back
edges.why: The second starts at 3, when the first ends. The test is start < end, so 3 < 3 is false and the room is reused.

edges.title: Empty schedule
edges.why: No meetings means no rooms. The loop never runs, so ends[e] is never read.

edges.title: Same slot three times
edges.why: Three meetings in the same slot are all running at once. Each needs its own room.

edges.title: One long meeting
edges.why: The short ones never overlap each other, so they share the second room one after another.

gotchas.text: Sort numbers with (a, b) => a - b. Plain sort() compares as strings, so [10, 9, 2] stays in that order, and the sweep then gives a wrong count.
Building starts and ends with intervals.map(...) makes new arrays, so sorting them leaves the input alone. Calling intervals.sort() directly would reorder the caller's data.
sort.Ints sorts numerically, which is what you want here. Build starts and ends with make and a loop, so sorting does not touch the caller's slice of slices.
Sorting starts and ends separately breaks the pairing on purpose. It is correct because the count of open meetings only depends on how many starts and ends came before a moment.
Use start < end to open a room. With <=, back-to-back meetings would be counted as needing two rooms.

recap.key: Sort starts and ends apart. A start before the earliest end opens a room; otherwise it reuses one.
recap.complexity: Time O(n log n). Space O(n).
moves: Sort all starts and all ends separately
For each start, compare it with the earliest unused end
If start < end, open a room (rooms + 1)
Otherwise reuse a room (move the end pointer)
